title: Arbitration and Conciliation Act s. 2 — Statutory provision (ACA s. 2)

content.overview: Section 2 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 contains the interpretive definitions used in the Act and sets the territorial/application framework for Part I and specified other provisions. The definitions must be applied in their statutory context, including the qualifications created by section 2(1) and the application provisions in section 2(2)–(5).

The correct analysis begins with the legal question and avoids replacing the governing enactment with a generic textbook summary.

2. Deconstruct definitions, conditions precedent, exceptions, provisos, explanations, jurisdictional limits and remedies.
3. Distinguish the topic from its nearest neighbour: Arbitration and Conciliation Act s. 1 — Statutory provision; Arbitration and Conciliation Act s. 3 — Statutory provision; Arbitration and Conciliation Act s. 4 — Statutory provision.
4. Apply the rule to the record and state which fact satisfies or fails each ingredient.

Competent forum: the competent civil court, arbitral tribunal, appointing court, supervisory High Court, or enforcement court according to the statutory stage and seat or venue. the party asserting the arbitration agreement, interim entitlement, award defect, settlement or enforcement objection must establish the procedural foundation from the contract and record. Where electronic records are relied upon, apply BSA 2023 s. 63 and the applicable burden provisions without treating electronic admissibility as proof of the ultimate fact. sections.heading: Section 2(1) — definitions
sections.body: Section 2(1) defines the principal expressions used in the Act, including arbitration, arbitration agreement, arbitral award, arbitral tribunal, court, international commercial arbitration, legal representative, party and specified references to a dispute. These are statutory definitions and should not be replaced by generic textbook meanings.

sections.heading: Arbitration and arbitration agreement
sections.body: The Act defines “arbitration” broadly by reference to whether or not it is administered by a permanent arbitral institution. “Arbitration agreement” is tied expressly to section 7. Accordingly, when analysing whether an agreement to arbitrate exists, section 2(1)(b) must be read together with section 7 rather than treated as a complete independent test.

sections.heading: Court and international commercial arbitration
sections.body: The statutory definition of “Court” identifies the judicial forum by reference to the relevant subject-matter and, in specified cases, the High Court. “International commercial arbitration” is defined by the statutory nationality/residence/incorporation/central-management criteria and the commercial character of the legal relationship. The exact statutory definition should be applied to the facts.

sections.heading: Sections 2(2)–(5) — application framework
sections.body: Section 2 is not confined to definitions. Its later sub-sections regulate the application of Part I and the relationship with other statutory or contractual arbitration arrangements. The applicable sub-section and its provisos must be checked before assuming that every Part I provision applies identically to every arbitration.

sections.heading: Context and current-law method
sections.body: Section 2 should be read with the current text of the Act and the provision governing the procedural step in issue. Historical amendments and judicial developments should not be silently substituted for the statutory wording. Where a definition contains alternatives or qualifications, each must be tested against the record.

provisions.title: Arbitration and Conciliation Act s. 2 — Statutory provision (ACA s. 2)

examples.title: Arbitration agreement
examples.body: A contract contains a clause referring defined disputes to arbitration. The existence and legal sufficiency of the arbitration agreement must be tested under section 7, while section 2(1)(b) supplies the statutory definition that links the expression to section 7.

examples.title: International commercial arbitration
examples.body: A commercial dispute involves a party satisfying one of the statutory foreign-party criteria. The court must apply every element of the section 2(1)(f) definition rather than treating any foreign connection as automatically sufficient.

examples.title: Court definition
examples.body: Before filing an application under the Act, identify the judicial forum specified by the statutory definition of “Court” and the provision under which the application is made. Do not assume that every arbitration application belongs in the same court.

hypotheticals.question: A party argues that any written reference to arbitration is automatically an arbitration agreement under section 2.
hypotheticals.analysis: Section 2(1)(b) defines the expression by reference to section 7. The existence and validity of the alleged agreement therefore require the section 7 analysis and the facts relevant to statutory incorporation or exchange.

hypotheticals.question: A dispute has an international element. Is it necessarily an international commercial arbitration?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Apply each statutory component of section 2(1)(f), including the relevant foreign status criterion and the commercial character of the legal relationship.

misconceptions.trap: Using a dictionary or textbook meaning instead of the statutory definition.
misconceptions.correction: Start with the exact definition in section 2 and read it with its contextual qualification.

misconceptions.trap: Assuming section 2(1)(b) alone proves an arbitration agreement.
misconceptions.correction: The definition expressly refers to section 7, so the agreement must be tested under section 7.

misconceptions.trap: Assuming every international element makes an arbitration an international commercial arbitration.
misconceptions.correction: Apply every statutory element of section 2(1)(f).

cases.name: Vidya Drolia v. Durga Trading Corporation
cases.facts: The Court considered arbitrability and the role of the referral court.
cases.issue: When should a court refer parties to arbitration and which disputes are non-arbitrable?
cases.ratioDecidendi: Referral scrutiny is limited, but the court must reject inherently non-arbitrable disputes and examine the arbitration agreement at the statutory threshold.
cases.holding: The Court formulated the modern Indian framework for arbitrability and referral.
cases.relevance: Use for arbitration agreement, referral and jurisdictional threshold questions.

cases.name: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC v. HSCC (India) Ltd.
cases.facts: The dispute concerned unilateral appointment power vested in an interested party.
cases.issue: Whether a person interested in the outcome may unilaterally appoint the sole arbitrator.
cases.ratioDecidendi: A person rendered ineligible to act as arbitrator cannot control the appointment process in a manner that creates justifiable bias.
cases.holding: The unilateral appointment mechanism was held invalid in the circumstances.
cases.relevance: Use for independence, impartiality and appointment challenges.

cases.name: Afcons Infrastructure Ltd. v. Cherian Varkey Construction Co. (P) Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court examined court-referred ADR under CPC s. 89.
cases.issue: How should courts select an appropriate ADR process?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The statutory ADR options must be applied according to the nature of the dispute and consent requirements.
cases.holding: The Court clarified the working scheme of CPC s. 89 and Order X.
cases.relevance: Use for mediation, conciliation and court-referred ADR.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should section 2 be used in an arbitration dispute?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Identify the statutory expression in issue, state its section 2 definition, read any contextual qualification and then apply the operative provision governing the dispute. For an arbitration agreement, section 2(1)(b) must be read with section 7.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: Definitions control statutory meaning but do not replace operative provisions.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What is the correct submission when a party relies on a generic meaning of a defined term?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: The Act supplies its own statutory definitions. The court should apply the definition in section 2, together with its contextual qualifications and the operative provision in which the term is used, rather than importing a generic meaning.

enhancement.definition: Section 2 supplies the Act's statutory definitions and its application framework.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: A statutory definition controls the meaning of the defined expression in the Act, subject to its contextual qualifications; an operative provision still supplies the legal conditions and consequences.
statutoryFramework: Section 7 — arbitration agreement, read with section 2(1)(b).
essentialIngredients: Apply the operative provision using the defined term.

enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 2 is foundational because the Act uses defined expressions throughout its arbitration and conciliation regimes. It includes the definition of arbitration and links arbitration agreement expressly to section 7. It also defines court and international commercial arbitration through statutory factual criteria. The later application provisions in section 2 prevent the definitions from being treated as the entire jurisdictional analysis. A sound approach is therefore definition first, contextual qualification second, operative provision third.

A commercial dispute involves a party satisfying one of the statutory foreign-party criteria. The court must apply every element of the section 2(1)(f) definition rather than treating any foreign connection as automatically sufficient.
